category: Core vocabulary: restaurants and dining out

entries.meaning: Restaurant food packed up to be eaten somewhere else. ---
examples: Let's just get carryout tonight.
The place does mostly carryout now.
Their carryout is cheaper than ordering delivery.
entries.contrast: Common in the Midwest; elsewhere Americans usually say takeout.

entries.meaning: A short menu of small, simple dishes for children. ---
examples: Do you have a kids' menu?
Everything on the kids' menu comes with fries.
The kids' menus double as coloring pages.

entries.meaning: A woman whose job is serving food and drinks at tables. ---
examples: Our waitress brought extra napkins without being asked.
She worked as a waitress all through college.
Two waitresses were covering the whole dining room.
entries.contrast: Most American restaurants now use the gender-neutral 'server' for the job.

entries.meaning: The largest dish of a meal, served after the appetizer. ---
examples: I had soup first and then a main course of grilled salmon.
Save room — the main course here is huge.
Both main courses came with mashed potatoes.
entries.contrast: Americans usually call this the entrée; in Britain an entrée is a starter.

entries.meaning: A smaller dish served alongside the main one. ---
examples: Rice comes as a side dish with every entrée.
We ordered three side dishes and shared everything.
The mac and cheese is a side dish, not a whole meal.

entries.meaning: A dish a restaurant offers on a particular day, often at a lower price. ---
examples: Tonight's special is blackened catfish.
Let me tell you about our specials.
The lunch special comes with soup and a drink.

entries.meaning: The running total of drinks a customer owes at a bar. ---
examples: Can I close out my bar tab?
He ran up a bar tab of ninety dollars.
They keep bar tabs open with a credit card.

entries.meaning: A set of items sold together for one price at a fast-food place. ---
examples: I'll take the number three combo with a Coke.
The combo costs less than buying it all separately.
They serve breakfast combos until eleven.
entries.contrast: Short for 'combination', but on American menus the short form is the normal word.

entries.meaning: Money added to a bill for the server's service. ---
examples: A gratuity of eighteen percent is added for parties of six or more.
The gratuity was already on the check.
Gratuities are split among the whole staff.
entries.contrast: The everyday word is 'tip'; gratuity is the formal one printed on checks and menus.

entries.meaning: A container on a counter where customers leave small change for the staff. ---
examples: He dropped a dollar in the tip jar.
The tip jar gets split at the end of the shift.
Most coffee shops keep tip jars right by the register.

entries.meaning: The amount on a bill before tax and tip are added. ---
examples: Tip on the subtotal, not on the total.
The subtotal came to forty-two dollars.
The receipt lists two subtotals, one for food and one for drinks.
entries.русский: промежуточный итог (сумма до налога и чаевых)

entries.meaning: A percentage the restaurant adds to the bill for service. ---
examples: A three percent service charge helps cover staff health care.
Check whether the service charge is already included before you tip.
Several cities have cracked down on surprise service charges.

entries.meaning: A fee charged at the door of a bar or club on top of food and drinks. ---
examples: There's a ten-dollar cover charge after nine.
The band plays free — no cover charge tonight.
Cover charges go up on the weekend.
entries.русский: плата за вход (в баре, клубе с музыкой)

entries.meaning: The machine that records sales and holds the money. ---
examples: Pay at the cash register by the door.
The cash register jammed in the middle of the lunch rush.
Both cash registers were open at noon.
entries.contrast: British speakers usually say 'till'.

entries.meaning: The desire to eat. ---
examples: All that walking gave me an appetite.
He lost his appetite after the bad news.
Teenagers have enormous appetites.

entries.meaning: The uncomfortable feeling of needing food. ---
examples: A handful of nuts took the edge off my hunger.
Hunger makes everything taste better.
She ate out of hunger, not out of pleasure.
entries.contrast: Uncountable: you feel hunger, but you have an appetite.

entries.meaning: The amount of food put on someone's plate at one time. ---
examples: He took a second helping of potatoes.
That's a generous helping for eight dollars.
There are enough helpings here for six people.

entries.meaning: A second serving of the same food. ---
examples: Does anybody want seconds?
He went back for seconds twice.
There's plenty of chili left if you want seconds.
entries.contrast: Used only in the plural in this sense — never 'a second' of food.

entries.meaning: A small extra dish ordered along with the main one. ---
examples: Can I get a side order of fries with that?
The side order of slaw is only two dollars.
We split a couple of side orders instead of getting entrées.

entries.meaning: The amount of food counted as one portion. ---
examples: The serving size is smaller than the picture suggests.
Check the serving size before you order two.
Restaurant serving sizes have grown over the years.

entries.meaning: The dish a restaurant or a cook is best known for. ---
examples: Crab cakes are the house specialty.
Ask the waiter what the kitchen's specialty is.
The menu lists a dozen regional specialties.
entries.contrast: Americans write specialty; the British write speciality, with an extra syllable.

entries.meaning: The dish most closely associated with a particular chef or restaurant. ---
examples: His signature dish is a slow-roasted duck.
Every good cook ends up with a signature dish.
The tasting menu included three of her signature dishes.
entries.contrast: The g is silent in 'sign' but clearly pronounced in signature: SIG-nuh-chur.

entries.meaning: The printed list of wines a restaurant sells. ---
examples: Could we see the wine list, please?
Their wine list runs to twelve pages.
Most of the wine lists around here are short and cheap.

entries.meaning: The list of drinks a restaurant or bar serves. ---
examples: Can we start with the drink menu?
The drink menu is printed on the back of the food menu.
They put out new drink menus every season.

entries.meaning: The separate list of sweet dishes brought after the meal. ---
examples: We were too full even to look at the dessert menu.
She brought the dessert menu without being asked.
Both dessert menus had the same chocolate cake.
entries.contrast: Dessert (dih-ZURT) has two s's; desert (DEZ-urt), the dry place, has one.

entries.meaning: A menu of dishes a restaurant will pack up for you to carry away. ---
examples: There's a stack of takeout menus in the kitchen drawer.
Grab the takeout menu and pick something.
Their takeout menu is shorter than the one in the dining room.

entries.meaning: A fixed series of small courses chosen by the chef. ---
examples: We splurged on the seven-course tasting menu.
The tasting menu takes about three hours.
Both tasting menus have a vegetarian version.

entries.meaning: A small place that sells coffee and light food. ---
examples: I work out of the coffee shop on Third Street.
There's a coffee shop on every corner downtown.
Two new coffee shops opened on the same block.

entries.meaning: A coffee shop where people sit for hours, often with music or readings. ---
examples: They read poetry at the coffeehouse on Friday nights.
The old coffeehouse still has the same wobbly chairs.
Greenwich Village coffeehouses were full of folk singers.

entries.meaning: A small, informal restaurant, usually French in style. ---
examples: There's a little bistro around the corner.
We had steak and fries at a bistro near the hotel.
Half the bistros in town are closed on Mondays.

entries.meaning: An informal word for any place that serves food. ---
examples: A new eatery opened where the bank used to be.
The strip has a dozen cheap eateries.
It's a family eatery, not fine dining.

entries.meaning: A place serving beer and simple food, often an old one. ---
examples: We stopped at a roadside tavern for burgers.
The tavern has been on that corner since 1890.
Colonial taverns served travelers and locals alike.

entries.meaning: A bar, especially an old-fashioned American one. ---
examples: The old saloon still has swinging doors.
He walked into the saloon and ordered a whiskey.
Frontier towns had more saloons than churches.

entries.meaning: A restaurant that specializes in beef. ---
examples: We took him to a steakhouse for his birthday.
The steakhouse downtown is expensive but worth it.
Chain steakhouses all serve the same cuts.
entries.contrast: Steak is said STAYK, rhyming with 'make', never with 'weak'.

entries.meaning: A shop or counter selling sandwiches, cold cuts, and prepared foods. ---
examples: The delicatessen on the corner makes a great pastrami sandwich.
She picked up potato salad at the delicatessen.
New York delicatessens are famous for piling the meat high.
entries.русский: гастроном, магазин готовой еды и закусок
entries.contrast: Almost always shortened to 'deli' in speech.

entries.meaning: A bar with big screens where people watch games and eat. ---
examples: We watched the playoffs at a sports bar.
Every sports bar in town was packed on Sunday.
The sports bar has forty TVs and decent wings.

entries.meaning: A bar that serves mostly wine, usually with small dishes. ---
examples: There's a wine bar two doors down.
We split a cheese board at the wine bar.
Several wine bars opened in the old warehouse district.

entries.meaning: A cheap, plain neighborhood bar. ---
examples: It's a dive bar, but the jukebox is great.
He knows every dive bar in the city.
The dive bars on that street are all closing.

entries.meaning: An outdoor area where beer and food are served at long shared tables. ---
examples: We spent the whole afternoon in the beer garden.
The beer garden opens as soon as it's warm.
German beer gardens seat hundreds of people.
entries.русский: пивной сад (открытая площадка с пивом и едой)

entries.meaning: A counter where customers build their own salad from a choice of ingredients. ---
examples: Lunch includes the salad bar.
He went back to the salad bar three times.
Some grocery stores have better salad bars than restaurants do.

entries.meaning: A small counter selling light food and drinks. ---
examples: There's a snack bar by the pool.
We grabbed hot dogs at the snack bar.
The snack bars close right after halftime.

entries.meaning: A counter where a chef makes sushi in front of the customers. ---
examples: We sat at the sushi bar and let the chef choose.
The sushi bar only seats eight people.
Most sushi bars here are open for lunch.

entries.meaning: A shop where ice cream is served to eat on the spot. ---
examples: The ice cream parlor has thirty flavors.
We walked to the ice cream parlor after dinner.
Old-fashioned ice cream parlors had marble counters and metal stools.
entries.contrast: Americans spell it parlor; the British spell it parlour.

entries.meaning: A large indoor space with many small food vendors and shared seating. ---
examples: The new food hall has twelve stalls under one roof.
We ate at the food hall in the train station.
Food halls have replaced a lot of old mall food courts.

entries.meaning: A small stand selling cooked food at a market or fair. ---
examples: The food stall at the market sells dumplings.
We ate standing up at a food stall on the sidewalk.
Rows of food stalls lined the fairgrounds.

entries.meaning: A long counter with stools where simple meals are served. ---
examples: He ate a grilled cheese at the lunch counter.
The old drugstore still has its lunch counter.
Downtown lunch counters were packed at noon.

entries.meaning: A cheap, plain diner serving fried food. ---
examples: It's a greasy spoon, but the eggs are perfect.
We stopped at a greasy spoon off the highway.
The old greasy spoons are being replaced by cafés.
entries.contrast: An affectionate nickname, not a complaint about the dishwashing.

entries.meaning: Truck stop has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We had pie at a truck stop in Nebraska.
The truck stop is open all night.
Truck stops usually have showers and a full diner.
We ate breakfast at a truck stop off I-80.
The best truck stops have showers and a laundry.
He filled up at the truck stop and kept going.

senses.head: A roadside place where drivers eat, refuel, and rest
examples: We had pie at a truck stop in Nebraska.
The truck stop is open all night.
Truck stops usually have showers and a full diner.

senses.head: A large highway stop with fuel, food and showers, used mainly by truck drivers
examples: We ate breakfast at a truck stop off I-80.
The best truck stops have showers and a laundry.
He filled up at the truck stop and kept going.

entries.русский: придорожная закусочная (для дальнобойщиков); стоянка для дальнобойщиков

entries.meaning: A booth selling food and drinks at a stadium, theater, or park. ---
examples: The line at the concession stand was twenty people deep.
Popcorn from the concession stand costs more than the ticket.
All the concession stands close after the seventh inning.
entries.русский: киоск с едой (на стадионе, в кинотеатре)

entries.meaning: A machine or counter that dispenses soft drinks. ---
examples: Refills are free at the soda fountain.
The soda fountain is out of root beer again.
Drugstores used to have soda fountains with swivel stools.
entries.русский: автомат с газировкой; стойка с газированными напитками

entries.meaning: A large room where a school or institution serves meals. ---
examples: Freshmen eat in the dining hall every night.
The dining hall closes at eight sharp.
Both dining halls were remodeled last summer.

entries.meaning: Cheap food prepared and served very quickly. ---
examples: We lived on fast food during the road trip.
Fast food is cheaper than cooking, but not by much.
He gave up fast food in January and lost ten pounds.
entries.contrast: Uncountable: a lot of fast food, never 'fast foods'.

entries.meaning: Expensive restaurant eating with formal service. ---
examples: This town has no fine dining to speak of.
She got her start in fine dining before opening a taco shop.
Fine dining usually means a dress code and a long wine list.

entries.meaning: Food sold from carts and stands on the sidewalk. ---
examples: The best street food in the city is on that block.
We ate street food for three days straight.
Street food is cheap, fast, and usually excellent.

entries.meaning: The business of preparing and serving meals to the public. ---
examples: She's worked in food service since high school.
Food service jobs are hard on your feet.
The company handles food service for three hospitals.

entries.meaning: A window where you order and pick up food without leaving your car. ---
examples: The drive-through line wrapped around the building.
We went through the drive-through on the way home.
Some banks and pharmacies have drive-throughs too.
entries.contrast: Usually spelled 'drive-thru' on American signs.

entries.meaning: A service in which staff bring your order out to your parked car. ---
examples: They offer curbside pickup until nine.
I ordered online and chose curbside pickup.
Half the restaurants on this street still do curbside pickup.
entries.русский: самовывоз к машине (заказ выносят на улицу)
entries.contrast: Americans write curb; the British write kerb for the same edge of the street.

entries.meaning: A small wheeled stand that sells food on the street. ---
examples: There's a food cart outside the office that sells tacos.
He runs a food cart downtown.
Food carts line the park at lunchtime.

entries.meaning: A restaurant where you park and eat in your car. ---
examples: The old drive-in still has carhops on roller skates.
We ate burgers at a drive-in outside of town.
Most of the drive-ins closed in the seventies.
entries.contrast: At a drive-in you park and stay; at a drive-through you never leave the line.

entries.meaning: Delivery fee has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The delivery fee is almost as much as the food.
They waive the delivery fee on orders over thirty dollars.
App delivery fees have gotten out of hand.
There's a five-dollar delivery fee on grocery orders.
The delivery fees add up fast.
They waived the delivery fee because the food was late.

senses.head: The extra charge for bringing an order to your door
examples: The delivery fee is almost as much as the food.
They waive the delivery fee on orders over thirty dollars.
App delivery fees have gotten out of hand.

senses.head: Money charged for bringing goods to the buyer
examples: There's a five-dollar delivery fee on grocery orders.
The delivery fees add up fast.
They waived the delivery fee because the food was late.

entries.meaning: An arrangement where customers order and pick up food at a counter rather than at a table. ---
examples: It's counter service, so order first and then grab a table.
Counter service keeps the prices down.
The place switched to counter service after the remodel.

entries.meaning: An arrangement where a server takes your order at the table and brings the food. ---
examples: The patio has table service after five.
There's no table service at lunch.
Table service means you're expected to tip.

entries.meaning: An arrangement in which customers help themselves instead of being waited on. ---
examples: The drink station is self-service.
Self-service keeps the line moving at lunch.
This cafeteria has been self-service for years.

entries.meaning: A list of customers waiting for a table. ---
examples: Put us on the waitlist for two, please.
The waitlist is about forty minutes long.
Both restaurants had waitlists out the door.

entries.meaning: A customer who arrives without a reservation. ---
examples: We're a walk-in, party of three.
They hold a few tables for walk-ins every night.
The restaurant takes walk-ins until nine.
entries.contrast: The l in walk is silent: WAWK-in.

entries.meaning: Someone who books a table and never comes. ---
examples: That eight o'clock reservation was a no-show.
They charge a fee for a no-show.
Friday nights always bring a few no-shows.

entries.meaning: A line of people waiting their turn. ---
examples: There was a queue out the door and around the corner.
We joined the queue for the buffet.
The queues move fast once they open the second register.
entries.contrast: Americans normally say 'line'; queue sounds British — and only the first letter is pronounced.

entries.meaning: The number a restaurant uses to identify each table. ---
examples: Give them your table number when you order at the counter.
The runner called out the wrong table number.
The table numbers stand in little metal holders.

entries.meaning: The fee a restaurant charges for opening wine you brought yourself. ---
examples: Corkage is twenty dollars a bottle.
They waive the corkage on Mondays.
Call ahead and ask about their corkage policy.
entries.русский: пробковый сбор (плата за открытие своей бутылки)

entries.meaning: A customer of a restaurant, bar, or shop. ---
examples: Patrons must be twenty-one to sit at the bar.
A regular patron complained about the music.
The sign asks patrons to wait to be seated.
entries.contrast: Said PAY-trun in American English, with the stress on the first syllable.

entries.meaning: A customer who comes to the same place often. ---
examples: He's a regular — they start his coffee when he walks in.
The bar's regulars all sit in the same seats.
Losing a regular hurts a small restaurant.

entries.meaning: The desk near the door where guests check in and wait to be seated. ---
examples: Wait at the host stand and someone will seat you.
The reservation book sits on the host stand.
Both host stands had lines backed up to the door.

entries.meaning: Someone with a keen interest in food and restaurants. ---
examples: My brother's a foodie — let him pick the place.
The neighborhood has become a foodie destination.
Foodies lined up for the new taco spot.

entries.meaning: A person who knows and cares a great deal about fine food. ---
examples: You don't have to be a gourmet to enjoy this.
The shop caters to gourmets and home cooks alike.
He's enough of a gourmet to send back a bad sauce.
entries.contrast: The t is silent and the stress falls on the second syllable: goor-MAY.

entries.meaning: A writer who reviews restaurants. ---
examples: A food critic came in last night and nobody recognized her.
The food critic gave the place three stars.
Food critics usually pay for their own meals.

entries.meaning: A person who owns and runs restaurants. ---
examples: The restaurateur opened his fourth place downtown.
She's a restaurateur, not a chef — she hires the cooks.
Local restaurateurs petitioned the city council.
entries.contrast: Spelled without the n of restaurant: restaurateur, not 'restauranteur'.

entries.meaning: A restaurant's wine expert, who advises guests and runs the cellar. ---
examples: The sommelier suggested a Rioja with the lamb.
Ask the sommelier for something under fifty dollars.
Two sommeliers work the dining room on weekends.

entries.meaning: The person in charge of a dining room, who greets and seats guests. ---
examples: The maître d' found us a table by the window.
Slip the maître d' twenty dollars and see what happens.
Good maître d's remember every regular's name.
entries.contrast: Short for maître d'hôtel, and said may-truh DEE.

entries.meaning: The chef who is second in command in a kitchen. ---
examples: The sous chef runs the line when the chef is off.
She spent two years as a sous chef before moving up.
Both sous chefs trained in France.
entries.contrast: Sous is French: it sounds like 'sue', with the final s silent.

entries.meaning: The chef in charge of a whole kitchen. ---
examples: The head chef rewrites the menu every season.
He was promoted to head chef at thirty.
Two head chefs left within a month of each other.

entries.meaning: The chef who makes the desserts and baked goods. ---
examples: Their pastry chef bakes the bread too.
The pastry chef trained in Paris.
Good pastry chefs are hard to find and harder to keep.
entries.contrast: Americans say PAY-stree; the British say PASS-tree.

entries.meaning: A cook who works one station on the kitchen line during service. ---
examples: He started as a line cook at nineteen.
The line cook on the grill quit mid-shift.
Line cooks work fast and stand up all night.
entries.русский: повар на линии (готовит на своей станции)

entries.meaning: A worker who clears and resets the tables. ---
examples: The busboy cleared our plates before we were finished.
He worked as a busboy all through high school.
Two busboys handle the whole dining room.
entries.contrast: The gender-neutral 'busser' is replacing busboy on American job listings.

entries.meaning: A worker who carries finished plates from the kitchen to the tables. ---
examples: A food runner brought our entrées out.
The food runner asked who had ordered the salmon.
Food runners never take the orders themselves.

entries.meaning: The servers of a restaurant, taken as a group. ---
examples: The waitstaff here is unusually good.
Half the waitstaff called in sick on Saturday.
They're hiring waitstaff for the summer.
entries.contrast: A collective noun: the waitstaff is friendly, with no plural 'waitstaffs'.

entries.meaning: An official who checks that a kitchen meets sanitation rules. ---
examples: The health inspector showed up unannounced.
A health inspector closed the place for a week.
Health inspectors make restaurants post the grade in the window.

entries.meaning: The rules about what customers may wear in a place. ---
examples: The restaurant has a dress code — no shorts, no sandals.
Check the dress code before you book.
Most dress codes were dropped years ago.

entries.meaning: A place near the entrance where guests leave their coats. ---
examples: Leave your jacket at the coat check.
The coat check is two dollars a coat.
Both coat checks are closed for the summer.

entries.meaning: The way a person behaves while eating with other people. ---
examples: His table manners are terrible.
She taught the kids table manners early.
Good table manners travel well.
entries.contrast: Always plural — there is no 'a table manner'.

entries.meaning: The mood a place creates through its lighting, sound, and decor. ---
examples: The food is fine, but the ambience is what sells it.
Candles give the room a warmer ambience.
You're paying for the ambience as much as for the meal.
entries.contrast: Also spelled 'ambiance'; both spellings are accepted in American English.

entries.meaning: The busiest stretch of the evening in a restaurant. ---
examples: Don't call me during the dinner rush.
The dinner rush starts around six thirty.
Friday and Saturday dinner rushes are brutal.
entries.русский: вечерний наплыв посетителей (час пик в ресторане)

entries.meaning: The announcement that a bar will take its final drink orders. ---
examples: Last call is at one thirty.
The bartender shouted last call and flipped the lights.
We ordered one more round right before last call.

entries.meaning: An arrangement at an event where the drinks are free to guests. ---
examples: The wedding had an open bar until ten.
An open bar gets expensive fast.
Open bars are rare at company parties now.

entries.meaning: An arrangement at an event where guests pay for their own drinks. ---
examples: Dinner is covered, but it's a cash bar.
They set up a cash bar in the lobby.
Cash bars keep the budget under control.
entries.русский: бар за свой счет (гости платят сами)

entries.meaning: A meal at someone's home with invited guests. ---
examples: We're hosting a dinner party on Saturday.
She's a nervous cook at dinner parties.
The dinner party ran until midnight.

entries.meaning: The hour at which a meal is usually eaten. ---
examples: Phones go away at mealtimes in this house.
The baby has a strict mealtime routine.
Mealtimes shift by an hour when we travel.

entries.meaning: An event at which people sample a series of wines or foods. ---
examples: We went to a wine tasting on Sunday afternoon.
The shop runs a cheese tasting every month.
Both tastings sold out in a day.

entries.meaning: A cool room where a restaurant or a home keeps its wine. ---
examples: The restaurant's wine cellar holds four thousand bottles.
He built a small wine cellar under the stairs.
Their wine cellars survived the fire.

entries.meaning: A substance in food that can cause an allergic reaction. ---
examples: The menu marks every common allergen.
Peanut is the allergen they worry about most.
Restaurants have to disclose eight major allergens.
entries.contrast: Stress falls on the first syllable, AL-ur-jun, unlike 'allergic'.

entries.meaning: A person who does not eat meat. ---
examples: I'm a vegetarian, so I'll take the pasta.
Is there anything here for a vegetarian?
Two of our guests are vegetarians.

entries.meaning: A person who eats no animal products at all. ---
examples: She's been a vegan for six years.
The place has a whole menu for vegans.
As a vegan, he skips the cheese and the butter.
entries.contrast: Said VEE-gun, not VEJ-un.

entries.meaning: Illness caused by eating contaminated food. ---
examples: Half the party got food poisoning from the shrimp.
It was a mild case of food poisoning.
Food poisoning can close a restaurant overnight.
entries.contrast: Uncountable: say 'a case of food poisoning', never 'a food poisoning'.

entries.meaning: A person's sense of taste, or their ability to judge flavors. ---
examples: He has a good palate for wine.
The sorbet clears your palate between courses.
A chef cooks for a lot of different palates.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like palette (an artist's board) and pallet (a wooden shipping platform).

entries.meaning: The flavor that stays in the mouth after eating or drinking. ---
examples: The coffee has a bitter aftertaste.
There's a nice smoky aftertaste to the ribs.
Diet sodas leave strange aftertastes.

entries.meaning: A small savory item served before a meal, usually with drinks. ---
examples: A waiter passed an hors d'oeuvre on a silver tray.
We filled up on hors d'oeuvres before dinner even started.
The caterer brought six kinds of hors d'oeuvres.
entries.contrast: French on the page, short in the mouth: or-DURV, with the plural said or-DURVZ.

entries.meaning: A tiny piece of bread or pastry with a topping, served at a party. ---
examples: A waiter came around with a tray of canapés.
She made a canapé with smoked salmon and dill.
The canapés disappeared in ten minutes.

entries.meaning: Small food meant to be eaten with the hands rather than with a fork. ---
examples: Serve finger food so people can keep mingling.
Everything at the party was finger food.
Toddlers do better with finger food.

entries.meaning: An alcoholic drink taken before a meal to sharpen the appetite. ---
examples: We had an aperitif out on the terrace.
A dry vermouth makes a good aperitif.
Aperitifs are on the first page of the drink menu.

entries.meaning: Booster seat has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Could we get a booster seat for her?
The booster seat straps onto a regular chair.
They keep booster seats stacked by the front door.
She moved out of the car seat and into a booster seat.
The restaurant brought a booster seat to the table.
We keep two booster seats in the trunk.

senses.head: A seat that raises a small child up to table height
examples: Could we get a booster seat for her?
The booster seat straps onto a regular chair.
They keep booster seats stacked by the front door.

senses.head: A cushion seat that lifts an older child so the seat belt fits
examples: She moved out of the car seat and into a booster seat.
The restaurant brought a booster seat to the table.
We keep two booster seats in the trunk.

entries.meaning: The table people sit at to eat a meal. ---
examples: The dining table seats eight comfortably.
We cleared the dining table to make room for the pie.
Long dining tables make a room feel communal.

entries.meaning: The part of a restaurant or home where people sit and eat. ---
examples: The dining area is through those doors.
They expanded the dining area onto the sidewalk.
Both dining areas were full by seven.

entries.meaning: A tall backless seat for sitting at a bar or high counter. ---
examples: He spun around on the bar stool.
There's one bar stool left down at the end.
The new bar stools actually have backs.

entries.meaning: A long upholstered bench running along a restaurant wall. ---
examples: We sat on the banquette by the window.
The banquette runs the whole length of the room.
Velvet banquettes give the place an old-fashioned feel.
entries.contrast: French-derived: said bang-KET, not 'BANK-wet'.

entries.meaning: The plate, glass, and utensils laid out for one person. ---
examples: There's a place setting missing at the end of the table.
Each place setting had three forks.
She bought twelve place settings of plain white china.

entries.meaning: The large flat plate a main course is served on. ---
examples: Put the salad on the small plate, not the dinner plate.
The dinner plate was barely big enough for the steak.
We only have six matching dinner plates left.

entries.meaning: The small plate at the left of a place setting for bread and butter. ---
examples: Your bread plate is the one on your left.
He set his roll on the bread plate.
The bread plates were cleared before the entrées came.

entries.meaning: A stemmed glass made for drinking wine. ---
examples: He knocked over a wine glass reaching for the bread.
Hold the wine glass by the stem, not the bowl.
The wine glasses came out of the dishwasher spotted.

entries.meaning: The plain glass a server keeps filled with water at a table. ---
examples: Could you refill my water glass?
The water glass left a ring on the table.
He filled all four water glasses at once.

entries.meaning: A tall straight glass holding a pint of beer. ---
examples: The beer comes in a pint glass.
He set the empty pint glass down on the bar.
They wash a thousand pint glasses on a good night.
entries.contrast: Pint looks like 'mint' but is said PYNT, with the vowel of 'mine'.

entries.meaning: A small cup with a handle for drinking tea. ---
examples: She poured the tea into a china teacup.
The teacup rattled against the saucer.
The good teacups are on the top shelf.

entries.meaning: The pitcher a server uses to refill water glasses. ---
examples: The busser came by with a water pitcher.
There's a water pitcher on every table.
They keep the water pitchers full of ice.

entries.meaning: A small container with holes for sprinkling salt. ---
examples: Could you pass the salt shaker?
The salt shaker is clogged again.
Salt shakers sit next to the ketchup on every table.

entries.meaning: A small container with holes for sprinkling ground pepper. ---
examples: The pepper shaker is empty again.
He shook the pepper shaker over his eggs.
The pepper shakers here are always full and the salt ones never are.

entries.meaning: A hand grinder that cracks whole peppercorns over a dish. ---
examples: The waiter came by with a giant pepper mill.
Give it two twists of the pepper mill.
Wooden pepper mills last for decades.

entries.meaning: A sauce or seasoning added to food at the table. ---
examples: Ketchup is the only condiment he ever uses.
The condiments are on the counter by the napkins.
Each table has a little rack of condiments.
entries.русский: приправа, соус (кетчуп, горчица и т. п.)

entries.meaning: A small paper envelope of sugar for coffee or tea. ---
examples: He emptied two sugar packets into his coffee.
There's a sugar packet stuck to the saucer.
The sugar packets are in the little dish by the creamer.
entries.contrast: Sugar begins with a 'sh' sound despite the s: SHUUG-ur.

entries.meaning: Toothpick has 2 distinct senses.
examples: There's a toothpick holding the sandwich together.
He grabbed a toothpick on his way out.
The olives came on little toothpicks.
He was chewing on a toothpick.
There's a jar of toothpicks by the register.
Use a toothpick, not your fingernail.

senses.head: A thin pointed stick for cleaning between the teeth or spearing food
examples: There's a toothpick holding the sandwich together.
He grabbed a toothpick on his way out.
The olives came on little toothpicks.

senses.head: A small pointed stick for getting food out from between the teeth
examples: He was chewing on a toothpick.
There's a jar of toothpicks by the register.
Use a toothpick, not your fingernail.

entries.meaning: The dishes, glasses, and utensils used for a meal. ---
examples: The restaurant replaced all its tableware last year.
They sell tableware on the second floor.
Chipped tableware goes straight into the trash.
entries.contrast: Uncountable: a lot of tableware, never 'tablewares'.

entries.meaning: The forks, knives, and spoons used at a table. ---
examples: Roll the flatware into napkins before service.
We're short on flatware tonight.
The flatware here is heavier than it looks.
entries.contrast: An American word; the British say cutlery. Both are uncountable.

entries.meaning: Knives, forks, and spoons taken together. ---
examples: The cutlery is in the drawer on the left.
Plastic cutlery comes with the takeout.
Set out enough cutlery for ten people.
entries.contrast: Americans normally say silverware or flatware; cutlery sounds British. Uncountable either way.

entries.meaning: Drinking glasses and other glass dishes as a group. ---
examples: The glassware comes out of the machine still wet.
They keep the good glassware up on the top shelf.
Half the glassware broke in the move.
entries.contrast: Uncountable: a piece of glassware, not 'a glassware'.

entries.meaning: The plates and bowls a meal is served on. ---
examples: They registered for plain white dinnerware.
The dinnerware is dishwasher safe.
Restaurant dinnerware has to survive a lot of abuse.

entries.meaning: Drinking glasses that stand on a stem. ---
examples: The stemware goes on the top rack.
She inherited a set of crystal stemware.
Wash the stemware by hand.

entries.meaning: Fine white ceramic dishes. ---
examples: We only use the good china at Thanksgiving.
A piece of china chipped in the sink.
The restaurant serves dessert on delicate china.
entries.contrast: Small c for the dishes; the country takes a capital C.

entries.meaning: A large spoon for dishing food out of a bowl onto plates. ---
examples: Stick a serving spoon in the rice.
The serving spoon is too big for that dish.
Put serving spoons next to each platter.

entries.meaning: A large bowl that food is brought to the table in. ---
examples: Pour the beans into a serving bowl.
The serving bowl went around the table twice.
Both serving bowls came back empty.

entries.meaning: A wide bowl for tossing and serving salad. ---
examples: Toss the greens in the big wooden salad bowl.
The salad bowl barely fit on the table.
They set out two salad bowls, one without dressing.

entries.meaning: A small covered bowl of sugar kept on the table. ---
examples: The sugar bowl is next to the creamer.
Somebody left a wet spoon in the sugar bowl.
Diner sugar bowls used to have a little metal flap.

entries.meaning: A large open bowl that a mixed drink is ladled out of at a party. ---
examples: Somebody spiked the punch bowl.
The punch bowl sat in the middle of the buffet.
They borrowed two punch bowls for the reception.

entries.meaning: A small covered dish that holds butter at the table. ---
examples: The butter dish is empty.
Pass the butter dish, please.
Their butter dishes all have little glass lids.

entries.meaning: A small boat-shaped pitcher for pouring gravy or sauce. ---
examples: Fill the gravy boat and put it on the table.
The gravy boat only comes out at Thanksgiving.
Two gravy boats made their way around the table.

entries.meaning: A small basket of bread brought to the table before the meal. ---
examples: They brought a bread basket and a dish of olive oil.
We went through three bread baskets waiting for the food.
The bread basket is free here.

entries.meaning: A deep bowl that soup is served in. ---
examples: He tipped the soup bowl to get the last spoonful.
The soup bowl sits on top of the dinner plate.
We're two soup bowls short for tonight.

entries.meaning: A large flat dish that food is carried to the table on. ---
examples: The turkey came out on a huge serving platter.
Warm the serving platter before you plate the fish.
The serving platters barely fit in the cabinet.

entries.meaning: A ring that holds a rolled cloth napkin at a place setting. ---
examples: Slide the napkin through the napkin ring.
Each napkin ring had a name card tied to it.
She collects old silver napkin rings.

entries.meaning: A sharp serrated knife brought out with a piece of meat. ---
examples: The server brought a steak knife with the ribeye.
This steak knife is dull.
The set came with six steak knives.
entries.contrast: Silent k in knife, and the plural turns the f into v: knives.

entries.meaning: A small blunt knife for spreading butter. ---
examples: Use the butter knife, not your steak knife.
The butter knife lies across the bread plate.
Butter knives aren't sharp enough to cut anything.

entries.meaning: A large round-bowled spoon for eating soup. ---
examples: The soup spoon goes on the far right.
She ate the chowder with a soup spoon.
We're missing two soup spoons from the set.

entries.meaning: The smaller fork used for the salad course. ---
examples: The salad fork is the short one on the outside.
He used the salad fork for his entrée by mistake.
Set out salad forks for all twelve guests.

entries.meaning: A metal pan kept warm over a small flame at a buffet. ---
examples: The scrambled eggs sat in a chafing dish.
Light the burner under the chafing dish.
A row of chafing dishes lined the buffet table.
entries.contrast: Chafing is said CHAY-fing, from 'chafe', not CHAF-ing.

entries.meaning: A rolling cart of sweets wheeled to the table after dinner.
examples: They rolled the dessert cart right up to our table.
Nobody can say no to the dessert cart.
Dessert carts are making a comeback.
